Is the “SUBTOTAL” on a later line than the one that has the the number?
Have you tried printing a few lines to see what they look like?
Incidentally, there’s no point in using the strip method before checking whether the line contains the substring because it won’t have any effect on whether that substring will be found. There’s also no need for the “else” because if the second condition is true, it’ll break out of the loop and not fall through to the following print line.

author: Rosuav
text:
Fred:

Thank you Matthew Barnett. The iter() worked. I did not know that function and now can use it on other areas I hope


Cool! Getting your head around the difference between iterables and iterators will definitely be worth it  A lot of things in Python are iterable - that is, you can use them in for loops - and when you do, you’re using an iterator to keep track of where you are in it. You want to iterate over a list? There’ll be a list iterator that remembers how far you’ve come. You want to iterate over a range? Yep, that thing’s called range_iterator. The important thing is, you can always explicitly get an iterator from something and then iterate over that. That way, instead of starting over every time, you start from where you left off, just like you did here.

author: tjreedy
text:
Year ago, I repeatedly used  with alternating skip and process loops, like Mathew said, to reduce 100s of lines of ascii output from a statistics programto perhaps a few dozen  Sometimes it was easier to detect the first process line instead of the last skip line.  So after a skip loop, with line a line to process, I instead did, not in Python, the equivalent of something like
while True:
    process(line)
    line = next(iter_lines)
    if skip(line): break

This assumes that it is easier t to detect the first line to skip again.
